newsitem.title: INDIA: South Asian nations agree to launch fresh talks.
newsitem.headline: South Asian nations agree to launch fresh talks.

text.p: South Asian nations on Tuesday agreed to launch a fresh round of negotiations on tariff concessions in July as a step towards creating a free trade area in the region.

The Committee on Economic Forum (CEC) agreed to start the deliberations in the Nepali capital Kathmandu in July. The CEC, a forum under the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), comprises commerce secretaries of the seven member countries.

"The CEC decided that the third round of negotiations would be launched in July 1997 at Kathmandu," Indian Commerce Secretary P.P. Prabhu told a news conference after a two-day meeting of the CEC in the Indian capital.

SAARC comprises the Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal, the Indian Ocean island nations of the Maldives and Sri Lanka, mostly Hindu India and its Moslem majority neighbours, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
SAARC took the first steps towards forming a trade bloc in 1995 with the creation of the South Asian Preferential Trading Arrangement (SAPTA), vowing to form a free-trade zone by the year 2005.
Two rounds of negotiations under SAPTA have already been completed under which member countries exchanged tariff concessions in 2,459 items.
SAFTA is the South Asian Free Trade Area planned by the member countries to start operating by the year 2000.
"The ultimate objective as mandated by the heads of the state government's of SAARC member countries is to estalbish SAFTA in the region by 2000 preferably but not later than 2005," Prabhu said.
The CEC also agreed to continue preferential treatment to the least devloped countries in the region and remove tariff barriers "as early as possible," he added.
"In the third round, an expert group will be constituted among member countries which will suggest the extent of product coverage for tariff consessions," Prabhu said.
The CEC agreed to exempt visa requirements for commerce ministers of south Asian nations, vice presidents of SAARC countries and certain other senior SAARC officials.
Prabhu said the CEC also agreed that a need to establish an "instutional mechanism" existed for settlement of trade disputes among businessmen of the region.
Intra-SAARC trade had grown substantially in the last few years but as a percentage of world trade was quite low, officials said.
